description: Nous sommes une équipe d’étudiants passionnés par l’observation de la Terre. Nous voulons utiliser les données satellites de la NASA pour proposer un outil de suivi de la qualité de l’air. Nous cherchons un développeur Python, une personne à l’aise avec la data et un profil design/communication. Nous travaillons à distance, en français et en anglais. Débutants bienvenus, l’essentiel est la motivation !
summary:
AgriRot is a responsive web app, installable on a phone, that helps farmers choose crops for their rotation. The farmer draws a field on a map, confirms the NASA climate data shown for it (POWER, IMERG, SMAP, NDVI), and adds soil, water, crop history, and priorities. AgriRot then compares three rotation strategies: the existing one, a recommended one, and an alternative.

It addresses the challenge directly. Each strategy explains why it is proposed, the evidence behind it, its benefits, the information gaps, and the risks to verify locally. Scenario sliders test resilience to less rain and higher temperatures, and a confidence level shows how reliable the inputs are. Scientific terms are explained simply, and the farmer's local knowledge always takes priority.

This matters because climate change makes rotation choices harder for farmers, especially smallholders. AgriRot turns satellite data into clear, honest guidance that supports the farmer's judgment without replacing it. Its core is global, with a first application near Yaounde, Cameroon.
details:
What it does and how it works

AgriRot is a responsive web app (installable on a phone) that helps a farmer choose which crop to add to a rotation. The farmer draws their field on a map, confirms the NASA climate data shown for it, and adds local information: soil, water access, the last three seasons, constraints, and priorities such as water saving, income, soil health, nitrogen, erosion, and fodder. AgriRot then compares three rotation strategies: the farmer's existing rotation, a recommended one, and an alternative with a different profile. For each strategy it shows why it is proposed, the evidence used, the benefits, the information gaps, and the risks that need local verification. The farmer can change a crop and see the plan recalculate, save fields, and share a farm with co-farmers.

Behind this, NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, and MODIS/VIIRS/Landsat NDVI are harmonized on a common monthly grid. A trapezoidal suitability function and a weighted geometric mean score each crop. Agronomic rules (e.g. no repeated botanical family, a legume after a cereal, no bare soil in the rainy season) are applied during a beam search over the seasons. Scenario sliders (rainfall −20%, temperature +2 °C) give a resilience index, and a confidence level reflects input quality.

Benefits

• Turns complex satellite data into readable indicators.

• Protects soil, saves water, and improves resilience to climate change.

• Every recommendation is explained, with its uncertainty shown.

• Terms such as NDVI, evapotranspiration, and soil moisture anomaly are explained in one sentence each, along with the difference between satellite and ground measurements.

Intended impact

Smallholder farmers make better-informed rotation decisions while keeping control. AgriRot supports the farmer's judgment and local expertise and does not replace them. The core is global and country-independent. The first application is the Yaoundé outskirts, Cameroon, and each new region only needs its own crop table and seasonal calendar.

Tools and technologies

• Frontend: React + Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet + Leaflet.draw + OpenStreetMap, Chart.js/Recharts, PWA.

• Backend: Python FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, SQLite, Shapely, JWT, Uvicorn.

• Data: Python (requests, pandas, numpy, xarray/netCDF4), Earthdata Search, Giovanni, Worldview, Jupyter.

• Model and ML: a standalone agrorot_core module (numpy, pandas), scikit-learn for climate trend forecasting (monthly normal + linear trend, tested against plain climatology), pytest.

• Crop data: FAO EcoCrop and GAEZ to build and verify the crop table.

• Collaboration: GitHub, Figma, Miro.

Creativity

• Three comparable strategies, each answering the challenge's five questions (why, evidence, benefits, gaps, local risks).

• Transparency built in: a confidence score, and a rule that if the ML does not beat the climatology baseline, we keep the baseline and say so.

• A farmer-first design in which the farmer's input takes priority over zone-level satellite data.

• A global core with local adaptation through region-specific crop files.

Factors our team considered

• Different data resolutions (POWER ~55 × 70 km), harmonized on one grid and honest about zone-level precision.

• The limits of satellite data (e.g. SMAP measures only the surface layer).

• The crop table values are indicative and need verification (IRAD, IITA), and thresholds and weights need calibration by an agronomist.

• Out of scope, so we don't over-promise: disease detection from photos, precise yield forecasts, offline use, and IoT sensors. AgriRot estimates risks and does not diagnose.

• Usability: tests with 2–3 people on phones, without help.
